prime.problem: Plain BFS to a goal d steps away explores a ball of radius d, and with b choices per step that ball holds about b<sup>d</sup> nodes. On a dictionary of words that's thousands of expansions for a 5-word ladder.
prime.fits: Fourth graph card. It is BFS from the previous card run twice, from both ends, and needs what that card gave: layer-by-layer frontiers and a seen set.
prime.goal: Run a two-ended BFS on Word Ladder, explain the b<sup>d</sup> vs 2·b<sup>d/2</sup> saving, and know when the trick doesn't apply.

attend: Why do two balls of radius d/2 contain so many fewer nodes than one of radius d?
Why grow the smaller frontier each step instead of strictly alternating, as the source does?
What exactly is checked in the meet test, and why does the first hit give the shortest ladder?
Which two properties must a problem have for a backward search to exist at all?

must: BFS ball grows like b<sup>r</sup> → two searches of radius d/2 → 2·b<sup>d/2</sup> nodes instead of b<sup>d</sup> → 2,000 vs 1,000,000 for b = 10, d = 6 in the model; 29 vs 1,606 words for cold → warm on a real word list
Work per step ≈ size of the frontier you expand → always expand the smaller side → a hub word on one side doesn't get re-expanded every other step → strict alternation is correct but slower
Needs one known goal + edges you can walk backwards → Word Ladder has both (one-letter changes are symmetric) → "any exit" goals or directed graphs without a reverse list rule it out
elevated: With edge weights the first meeting is not always cheapest → the simple meet test is wrong for bidirectional Dijkstra → A* is usually used instead
reference: neighbour generation by trying 26 letters at each position
the source's two-Tree class and child_parents for Word Ladder II

compress.prompt: From memory, write the hit → cog trace as four rows (which side grows, new words, other frontier, ladder length) and explain in two sentences why the answer is 5.
checklist: step 1 grows hit → hot; step 2 grows hot → dot, lot
step 3 grows the smaller side, cog → dog, log
step 4: dog's neighbour dot is on the other frontier → meet
the shared seen set means each word joins a frontier once

retrieve.q: Explain why meeting in the middle saves work exponentially, using the ball-growth model, and why real word graphs don't match the model exactly.
answer: one search explores about b<sup>d</sup>; two explore about 2·b<sup>d/2</sup>
the ratio is b<sup>d/2</sup>/2: 500× for b = 10, d = 6
real graphs are lumpy (hubs, dead ends), so the card measures on a real list: 55× for cold → warm

retrieve.q: Walk through step 3 of the hit → cog trace: which frontier is grown, why, and what is compared against what?
answer: hit's side has 2 words (dot, lot), cog's side has 1
so the frontiers are swapped and cog's side grows: dog, log
each new word is checked against hit's frontier; no hit yet, so the ladder is at least 5

retrieve.q: For Word Ladder II (every shortest ladder), why can't you stop at the first meeting, and what does finishing the layer cost?
answer: other shortest ladders may meet through different words in the same layer
finish the whole meeting layer and keep every parent of each word
extra work: one more full layer and a parent list per word

compare.q: Both A* and bidirectional BFS explore fewer nodes than BFS toward one known target. Where does each get its savings, and which one survives when edges have weights?
answer: bidirectional: splits the radius between two balls; needs reversible edges
A*: steers one search with a lower-bound estimate h; needs a good heuristic
with weights, A* keeps its optimality with a consistent h; the simple bidirectional meet test breaks

compare.q: On the 6-word list plain BFS expands 6 words and two-way expands 4. Why is the saving tiny there and 55× on the 4,360-word list?
answer: the saving grows with b<sup>d/2</sup>; the small graph has few branches
the big list has many words one letter apart, so the one-way ball is huge
on small graphs plain BFS is simpler and the difference is noise

predict.q: Remove "cog" from the word list. Predict what the two-way search returns and how many steps it takes to notice.
predict.answer: It returns 0 at once: the goal isn't in the word set, so the function exits before searching (if end not in words: return 0). If the goal were present but unreachable, the search would stop when one frontier runs dry, which is why the loop condition is while front and back.

apply.task: Turn the word-ladder search into Minimum Genetic Mutation: letters ACGT, answer = ladder words − 1, and −1 when no ladder exists. Run it on start AACCGGTT, end AAACGGTA, bank ["AACCGGTA", "AACCGCTA", "AAACGGTA"].
apply.done: Your function returns 2 on that input and −1 when the end isn't in the bank; it never calls an undefined helper (the source's bug).
apply.hint: Only the alphabet and the final subtraction change; the two-frontier loop stays the same.
